Universally attributed to Dōgen Zenji across quote databases (AZQuotes, Goodreads, etc.), but no specific chapter or fascicle of the Shobogenzo has been confirmed as the source in any search result found. 'Enlightenment is intimacy with all things' reads as an interpretive paraphrase or secondary synthesis rather than a direct translation. The Shobogenzo (1231–1253) is the canonical primary source for Dōgen, but this exact phrasing cannot be pinned to a specific fascicle without further scholarly verification. Plausible but unconfirmed.

Quote Investigator (quoteinvestigator.com/2020/05/13/make-friends/) investigated this thoroughly and concluded: 'based on current evidence this anecdote is apocryphal.' The saying has been attributed to Abraham Lincoln (via a post-mortem Civil War anecdote), Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund (d. 1437), and Mark Twain — all attributions appearing long after each figure's death. An 1867 New Orleans newspaper attributed a similar saying to Sigismund; the Lincoln anecdote form emerged by the 1940s. An 1858 Wisconsin newspaper cited the concept in relation to Cardinal Richelieu. An 1885 Vermont newspaper printed a similar line with no attribution. No primary Lincoln source (speech, letter, diary) has ever been found. The attribution to Lincoln is not credible.

results.earliest_print_source: The Story of Philosophy, Will Durant, Simon & Schuster, 1926
results.notes: The pre-flag is correct and this is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The sentence is Will Durant's own summarizing gloss on the Nicomachean Ethics (roughly 1103a-b, on virtue as hexis acquired by habituation), written in The Story of Philosophy (1926). Aristotle never wrote it; Durant's line is set immediately after his paraphrase of Aristotle and the quotation marks migrated over time. Wikiquote lists it under Aristotle's misattributed section. Recommend crediting Durant and, if the Aristotelian idea is wanted, citing Nicomachean Ethics directly instead.

results.earliest_print_source: John M. Culkin, "A Schoolman's Guide to Marshall McLuhan," Saturday Review, 18 March 1967

Culkin wrote "We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us" while summarizing McLuhan's argument; McLuhan himself did not write the sentence in this form. Two cautions: (a) the corpus text "thereafter our tools shape us" is a later smoothing of Culkin's wording — consider restoring the original; (b) the line is often confused with Churchill's "We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us" (House of Commons, 28 October 1943), which is a genuinely separate quotation and a likely source of the "thereafter" construction.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Maslow, and entirely consistent with his writing on creativeness in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971), where he discusses spontaneity and play in primary creativity. Plausibly genuine, unsourced.

Watts read and quoted Eckhart constantly, so he may well have said this in a lecture, but he would have been relaying it, not coining it. Attributing it to Watts as author is likely wrong. My confidence in Eckhart as the formulator is moderate rather than high, hence the hedge.

I am recalling the July 1839 date from memory and have not re-checked it against the printed Journal, so the date carries slightly more uncertainty than the attribution itself.

results.earliest_print_source: Walden; or, Life in the Woods, Henry David Thoreau, 1854, ch. 2 ("Where I Lived, and What I Lived For")
results.notes: Both fragments are genuine and come from the same famous passage in Walden ch. 2, but the ellipsis compresses several sentences. Thoreau's text runs: 'Our life is frittered away by detail... Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three... Simplify, simplify.' The condensation is faithful in sense but is not a contiguous quotation; if the corpus wants an exact citation, either restore the full passage or quote 'Simplify, simplify' on its own.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations in Wall Street, Henry Stanley Haskins, 1940
results.notes: The first sentence is a well-documented misattribution. Quote Investigator traced 'What lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters compared to what lies within us' to Henry Stanley Haskins's anonymously published Meditations in Wall Street (1940); it is usually pinned on Emerson, sometimes on Thoreau or Oliver Wendell Holmes, and appears in the Misattributed section of Emerson's Wikiquote page. The second sentence ('And when you bring what is within out into the world, miracles happen') is a later accretion with no source at all — it is not in Haskins and not in Thoreau. The author field's hedge, 'Transcendentalist insight inspired by Henry David Thoreau,' is an invented byline; nothing here is Thoreau's. Recommend rejecting rather than reattributing, since the composite sentence as quoted matches no single source.
results.suggested_reattribution: Henry Stanley Haskins (first sentence only; second sentence has no known source)

results.earliest_print_source: Plato, Apology 38a (c. 399–390 BCE)
results.notes: Socrates' words as reported by Plato at his trial, Apology 38a: 'ho de anexetastos bios ou biotos anthropoi' — the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being. Standard, uncontested, and the single best-sourced Socrates quotation. Strictly speaking it is Plato's rendering of Socrates, who left no writings, but the attribution convention is universal.

This exact English sentence is a modern aphorism, not a translation of anything in Plato or Xenophon. The underlying idea is genuinely Socratic — the paradox 'no one errs willingly' (oudeis hekon hamartanei), argued in Protagoras 345d-e and developed in Meno and Gorgias, that wrongdoing is a form of ignorance rather than deliberate choice. But the compressed one-liner phrasing is contemporary and I cannot place who first put it this way. Defensible as a paraphrase clearly labeled as such; not defensible as a Socrates quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book 2.11; this English wording from Gregory Hays's translation (Modern Library, 2002)
results.notes: Genuine, from Meditations 2.11. The crisp modern phrasing is specifically Gregory Hays's 2002 translation; older translations render it very differently (Long: 'Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly'). Worth crediting the translator if the corpus surfaces translation credits.

Consistently attributed to Shunryu Suzuki and, to my recollection, drawn from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind (Weatherhill, 1970), where the theme that practice is not preparation for a later attainment is central. I cannot confirm the chapter or page from memory, and the two sentences may be a condensation of a longer passage rather than a contiguous quotation, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting a locus I cannot check. The attribution itself is unlikely to be wrong; the citation is what is missing.

One of the most persistent Churchill misattributions. The International Churchill Society lists it among quotes falsely attributed to him: it appears nowhere in his speeches, books, or recorded remarks, and Churchill's own Wikiquote page files it under Misattributed. Variants of the underlying saying ('success is never final and failure never fatal') circulated in American motivational, business, and sportswriting from roughly the late 1930s onward, with no consistent author; the 'courage to continue' clause appears to be a later addition. I cannot identify a genuine originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution. Should not go live under Churchill's name.

Widely circulated as Picasso, almost always without any citation, and I know of no primary source — no interview, letter, or recorded remark. Picasso is a moderate misattribution magnet for epigrams about art and time. The line's idiom feels like late-20th-century American self-help/productivity writing rather than a translation from Picasso's French or Spanish, which further weakens the attribution. Honest answer: origin unknown, Picasso unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: De Brevitate Vitae (On the Shortness of Life), Seneca, c. 49 CE, ch. 14; this English wording from C. D. N. Costa's translation (Penguin, 1997)
results.notes: Genuine and correctly transcribed. This is the opening of De Brevitate Vitae 14, Seneca's argument that the philosopher annexes all past ages to his own lifetime. The English is C. D. N. Costa's Penguin translation, whose distinctive phrasing ('they annex every age to theirs', 'in loftiness of mind to pass beyond the narrow confines of human weakness') matches this text closely. Note the corpus context field says 'Ancient Greek' — Seneca was Roman and wrote in Latin.

results.earliest_print_source: Pro Plancio, Cicero, 54 BCE, §80
results.notes: Genuine Cicero, from the defense speech Pro Plancio: 'haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima, sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum' — this is the one virtue that is not only greatest but the parent of all the rest, said of gratitude. The English is the standard rendering found in quotation dictionaries. Section number 80 is from memory. Note the corpus context field says 'Ancient Greek'; Cicero was Roman.

The sentiment is squarely Ciceronian and matches the central argument of De Officiis Book III — that nothing dishonorable can genuinely be expedient, and that apparent utility gained through wrongdoing is not utility at all. But I cannot pin this English sentence to a specific passage, and I am not confident it renders a single Latin line rather than summarizing the argument. Plausible but uncited; do not promote without a checked locus in De Officiis. Corpus context field again wrongly lists Cicero as Greek.

I know of no such sentence anywhere in the Platonic corpus, and the 'an hour of X versus a year of Y' construction is a modern rhetorical shape, not a Greek one. It is sometimes defended as a gloss on Republic 536e-537a, where Socrates says children should be taught through play rather than compulsion — but that passage is about pedagogy, not about reading character, so the gloss does not hold. Plato is a heavy misattribution magnet for aphorisms of this kind. No genuine originator identifiable.

A modern condensation rather than a translation. The idea is authentically Epictetan and comes from Encheiridion 46, where he says not to call yourself a philosopher or talk about your principles among laymen, but to act on them — with the image of sheep that do not bring up grass to show the shepherd how much they ate, but produce wool and milk instead. No standard translation (Long, Higginson, Oldfather, Hard) contains this two-sentence English form; it reads like the loose contemporary paraphrase tradition around Epictetus. Safe to use if labeled a paraphrase of Encheiridion 46; not safe as a direct quotation.

results.earliest_print_source: Encheiridion (The Manual), Epictetus, c. 125 CE, §5
results.notes: The locus is certain: Encheiridion 5, the most quoted line in the whole handbook. Standard translations run 'Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things' (Long) or 'It is not events that disturb people, it is their judgements concerning them' (Hard). The wording here is a loose modern rendering rather than any established translation, so the attribution is solid while the exact phrasing is editorial. Consider aligning the text with a named translation.

results.earliest_print_source: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Seneca, Letter 13.4 (c. 65 CE)
results.notes: Genuine, from Letter 13, 'On Groundless Fears'. Gummere's Loeb translation reads: 'There are more things likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.' The quoted form drops 'often', which slightly strengthens the claim but does not distort it. Well documented and correctly attributed.

results.earliest_print_source: Meditations, Marcus Aurelius, Book 11.18 (c. 170–180 CE)
results.notes: Genuine, from the long passage in Meditations 11.18 on how to respond to people who wrong you, which closes on the claim that gentleness or kindness cannot be defeated when it is sincere — Hays renders it 'Kindness is invincible, provided it's sincere'. Translations split between 'gentleness' and 'kindness', so the three-word form here is a compression of a conditional sentence: Marcus qualifies it with 'if it be genuine'. Attribution is sound; the aphoristic trimming drops that qualifier.

results.earliest_print_source: De Tranquillitate Animi (On Tranquility of Mind), Seneca, c. 60 CE, §15
results.notes: Genuine Seneca, from the section of On Tranquility of Mind comparing Democritus, who laughed at human folly, with Heraclitus, who wept over it — Seneca sides with Democritus and says it better befits a man to laugh at life than to lament it. The English matches the Basore Loeb rendering closely. Section 15 is from memory; the work and the argument are certain.

Two separate issues. First, the author name is misspelled — 'Epectitus' should be 'Epictetus'. Second, this is a modern paraphrase, not a translation. The thought corresponds to Encheiridion 20: it is not the man who reviles you who insults you but your own judgement that the thing is insulting, so when someone provokes you it is your own opinion that has provoked you. The word 'complicit' and the whole register belong to the contemporary loose-paraphrase tradition around Epictetus (Sharon Lebell's The Art of Living, 1995, popularized renderings of exactly this kind), not to Long, Oldfather, or Hard. Usable if labeled a paraphrase of Encheiridion 20.
results.suggested_reattribution: Epictetus (spelling correction only, not a change of author)

results.notes: Attributed to Epictetus consistently in English quotation dictionaries going back to the nineteenth century, and the theme is the backbone of Discourses Book IV.1 ('On Freedom'), where he argues that the free man is the one who lives as he wishes and is enslaved by his own desires if by nothing else. But I cannot match this sentence to a specific passage, and the aphorism is close enough to Seneca's 'nemo liber est qui corpori servit' (Letter 92) that the two may have cross-contaminated in the quotation tradition. Plausible and old, but uncited; do not promote without a checked locus.

results.earliest_print_source: Encheiridion (The Manual), Epictetus, c. 125 CE, §8
results.notes: Genuine, from Encheiridion 8, one of the best-known lines in the handbook: do not seek to have events happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do, and your life will go well. The phrasing here is a variant translation rather than the standard Long or Hard wording, but it renders the same sentence and the locus is not in doubt.

I cannot match this to any chreia in Diogenes Laertius Book VI, which is the main source for sayings of Diogenes of Sinope, nor to any other ancient collection I know. The sentiment — that an insult disgraces the person who delivers it rather than its target — is a commonplace across ancient moral philosophy (compare Seneca's De Constantia Sapientis and Epictetus, Encheiridion 20), which makes a confident attribution to any one figure unsafe. Two further problems: 'infers' is almost certainly a corruption of 'offers' or 'utters', and the corpus context field labels Diogenes a Stoic when he was the founding Cynic. No true originator identifiable.

results.earliest_print_source: Vatican Sayings (Sententiae Vaticanae) 52, Epicurus (collection preserved in a Vatican Greek manuscript, first published 1888)
results.notes: Genuine Epicurus, Vatican Sayings 52 — commonly translated 'Friendship dances around the world, announcing to each of us that we must awaken to happiness' or 'bidding us all to awaken to the recognition of blessedness'. The wording here is a standard variant translation. One correction needed: the author is spelled 'Epicurius' in the input; it should be 'Epicurus'. The context field labels him Epicurean and Greek, which is right.
results.suggested_reattribution: Epicurus (spelling correction only, not a change of author)

results.notes: Consistently attributed to Schopenhauer and, to my recollection, drawn from the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life in Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), whose argument that what a man is in himself contributes far more to his happiness than what he has or how he is regarded matches this line exactly. I cannot confirm the chapter or the translator from memory, and the crisp English balance of 'difficult... impossible' may be a translator's or anthologist's polish rather than a literal rendering, so I am leaving the print source null. Attribution likely correct, citation unconfirmed.

Attributed to Schopenhauer with unusual consistency, largely because Erwin Schrodinger quoted it in his own work and gave it wide currency in scientific writing. I believe the attribution is genuine, but I cannot place the primary work — it is usually said to come from Schopenhauer's manuscript remains (Nachlass) rather than from a published book, which is exactly the kind of claim that gets repeated without checking. Also frequently seen in a shorter form ('The task is not to see what no one has yet seen, but to think what nobody has yet thought about what everybody sees'). Sound enough to keep, not sound enough to present as sourced.

results.earliest_print_source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. II, Ch. 31 ('On Genius'), Arthur Schopenhauer, 1844
results.notes: Genuine Schopenhauer. The German original runs roughly 'Das Talent gleicht dem Schuetzen, der ein Ziel trifft, welches die Uebrigen nicht erreichen koennen; das Genie dem, der eines trifft, bis zu welchem sie nicht einmal zu sehen vermoegen' — from the supplementary volume of Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung (1844), chapter on genius. The English wording here is the standard condensed rendering rather than a literal translation of Payne or Haldane/Kemp, so the sense is Schopenhauer's but the phrasing is a popular paraphrase. Attribution itself is not in doubt.

Lennon is the weakest of the three candidate attributions. The saying is far more commonly credited to Yoko Ono, and it drifted onto Lennon posthumously the way many Ono lines did. A closely parallel and earlier documented line belongs to Dom Helder Camara — 'When we are dreaming alone it is only a dream. When we are dreaming with others, it is the beginning of reality' — from The Desert Is Fertile (1974). I cannot confirm from memory whether Ono's version predates or derives from Camara's, so I am not asserting a print source. What I am confident about is that the John Lennon attribution has no support I know of.
results.suggested_reattribution: Yoko Ono

results.notes: Consistently and exclusively attributed to Ram Dass, with no competing claimant I am aware of, and entirely idiomatic of his teaching voice. Like much of his circulating material it appears to come from recorded talks and satsang transcripts rather than a book I can name, so I cannot give a print citation. Attribution plausible-to-likely; source unlocated.

The famous case of an unlocatable attribution. The Institute for Intercultural Studies, which Mead herself founded, stated that it could not locate the quotation in her published writing, while noting the sentiment is consistent with her views and may come from an interview or informal remark. No primary source has ever been produced despite decades of searching. Author is plausible; documentation is absent.

Circulates as Merton, usually in the form 'A man who fails well is greater than one who succeeds badly.' The thought is congruent with Merton's writing on failure and false success, and I know of no rival attribution, but I cannot place it in a specific book — I would be guessing between No Man Is an Island, The Sign of Jonas, and the essay collections, so I am naming none of them.

Consistently attributed to Merton and characteristic of his writing on dialogue and mutual truth. I do not have a reliable memory of which volume it comes from — Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander is my hunch but not a knowledge claim, so I am leaving the print source null rather than risk laundering a guess into a citation.

Genuine Merton in substance and phrasing; the interdependence-as-ground-of-compassion theme runs through his late Buddhist-facing work, and the wording matches his prose closely enough that I doubt it is a paraphrase. Commonly cited to Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander (1966), and sometimes to the Asian journal material, but I cannot resolve between them from memory, so no print source asserted.

results.earliest_print_source: No Man Is an Island, Thomas Merton, 1955
results.notes: One of the best-documented Merton passages. The standard citation in scholarly and popular references alike is No Man Is an Island (Harcourt, Brace, 1955), from the opening material on love, and the quoted text matches Merton's published wording. I am confident in book and year from memory of the standard reference; I have not verified a page number and am not supplying one.

results.earliest_print_source: Auguries of Innocence, William Blake, written c. 1803, first published 1863 in Gilchrist's Life of William Blake
results.notes: The opening quatrain of Auguries of Innocence, from the Pickering Manuscript. Attribution is beyond dispute. Two transcription defects in the corpus text should be fixed before publication: 'infintiy' is a typo for 'infinity', and Blake's text reads 'a Wild Flower' (two words) not 'a wildflower'. Blake's line breaks are four lines, not two; the canonical text is 'To see a World in a Grain of Sand / And a Heaven in a Wild Flower, / Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand / And Eternity in an hour.'

The author is right but the wording is a modern compression. Churchill's documented line, from a wartime minute, runs: 'The maxim Nothing avails but perfection may be spelt shorter — Paralysis.' That is the genuine article; 'Perfectionism spells paralysis' is a paraphrase that circulates in business and productivity writing. I recall the minute being reproduced in the appendices of The Second World War but cannot pin the volume, so no print source asserted. Also note the author field misspells the name — it should be 'Winston Churchill', not 'Churchil'. Churchill is a known misattribution magnet, but here the underlying attribution is sound; only the phrasing is secondhand.

results.earliest_print_source: Discourses, Book I, Ch. 2, Epictetus (recorded by Arrian, c. 108 CE)
results.notes: This tracks a real passage in Discourses I.2, where Epictetus argues from the athlete's example that we do not abandon a discipline out of despair of ever being the best at it. Translations vary considerably and the corpus wording matches no standard translation I know (Long, Oldfather, Hard), so treat it as a loose modern rendering rather than a quotation. Confidence is in the attribution to Epictetus, which I hold as strong; the exact English is not his translator's. Also note the author field misspells the name — it should be 'Epictetus', not 'Epectitus'.

Very widely circulated as Warhol, almost always without a citation. I cannot place it in The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), POPism (1980), or the published diaries, which is where a line this quotable would be expected to sit. The register also reads more like contemporary creative-advice writing than Warhol's clipped, deadpan speech. I do not have evidence identifying a true author, so I am not proposing a reattribution — but the attribution should be treated as unsupported.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Guts of a New Machine', Rob Walker, The New York Times Magazine, 30 November 2003
results.notes: Jobs said this to Rob Walker in the New York Times Magazine piece on the iPod. The fuller passage runs 'Most people make the mistake of thinking design is what it looks like... That's not what we think design is. It's not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.' The condensed form quoted here is faithful to the sense and is the version that entered general circulation.

Consistently attributed to Jobs and consistent with his stated posture on killing products quickly. My recollection places it in an interview rather than a speech — a Fortune profile from the late 2000s is my impression — but I cannot fix the outlet or date with enough confidence to name one, so the print source stays null. No competing attribution known.

results.earliest_print_source: Apple Worldwide Developers Conference closing Q&A, Steve Jobs, May 1997
results.notes: From the well-known WWDC 1997 fireside/Q&A session Jobs held shortly after returning to Apple — the same session that produced the 'start with the customer experience and work backwards to the technology' answer. The passage is widely reproduced from the recording and is also quoted in Isaacson's biography. I am confident in the venue and year; the exact date within the conference I have not verified.

results.earliest_print_source: Stanford University Commencement Address, Steve Jobs, 12 June 2005
results.notes: Verbatim from the third story ('about death' — actually this passage closes the second story, on love and loss) of the Stanford commencement address. Full text is published by Stanford and the video is a matter of record. Attribution and wording both solid.

Ubiquitous as a Disney quotation, including in Disney-affiliated merchandise and park signage, but I know of no primary source — no interview, memo, speech, or contemporaneous account. Late-appearing attributions of this kind to Disney are common. The sentiment is unobjectionable and no rival author is known to me, so I am not calling it apocryphal, but it should not clear a verification bar.

Long and consistently attributed to Bell, and it appears in older quotation compendia rather than only in modern internet collections, which is a point in its favour — many bogus attributions have no pre-web trail at all. I cannot name the speech, letter, or article it came from, so no print source is asserted. Attribution likely; documentation unlocated.

Marysarah Quinn is a real person — a book designer and creative director in trade publishing — and the obscurity of the name is mildly reassuring, since invented attributions gravitate toward famous names rather than away from them. But I cannot place this line in anything she wrote or is recorded as saying. My impression is that it entered circulation via an anthology or an essay quoting her in conversation, which I cannot confirm. Honest answer: I don't know.

'Ian Wallace' here is not an author but a fictional character — the line is spoken by Ian Wallace (played by Oliver James) in the 2003 film What a Girl Wants, and the credit therefore belongs to the screenwriters, Jenny Bicks and Elizabeth Chandler, working from the play The Reluctant Debutante. The quote is also frequently and wrongly attributed to Dr. Seuss, which is a separate and clearly false attribution. Recommend either recrediting to the film or dropping the item, since attributing dialogue to a character as if he were a person is misleading.

results.notes: Firmly associated with Ella Baker and adopted as the motto of the Ella Baker Center for Human Rights, which is meaningful secondary support. One caveat worth recording: Baker is understood to have used the line as an existing adage rather than coined it, so 'Ella Baker said this' is well supported while 'Ella Baker originated this' may not be. I cannot name the speech or interview in which she used it.

results.earliest_print_source: Upstream: Selected Essays, Mary Oliver, 2016
results.notes: From Oliver's essay collection Upstream, where it appears in her discussion of attention as the ground of a devoted life. The line is quoted from that book widely and correctly. I am confident in book and year; page unverified.

Genuine Thich Nhat Hanh in substance — this is his well-known verse on no-birth and no-death, which he wrote for use at funerals and which the Plum Village community recites. It is commonly cited to No Death, No Fear (2002), and I believe it appears there, but the wording here differs from the version I recall ('This body is not me. I am not caught in this body. I am life without boundaries. I have never been born and I have never died...'), so this looks like a variant translation or an abridgement. Attribution to Thich Nhat Hanh is strong; the specific text and its source edition are not confirmed, hence no print citation.

Idiomatic of Mooji and consonant with his 'be nothing, know nothing, have nothing' teaching, and I know of no competing attribution. But his material circulates almost entirely as satsang transcripts and social-media cards, and I cannot place this aphorism in a specific book or recorded talk. Plausible but undocumented in my knowledge.

Same situation as the companion Mooji item. The line reads as authentic Mooji and no rival author is known to me; my impression is that it belongs to the aphorism collections such as White Fire (2014), but that is an impression rather than a recollection I can stand behind, so no print source is given. Living teachers' quotations are hard to verify without a recording or a page reference, and I have neither.

Consistently attributed to Wei Wu Wei (pen name of Terence Gray, 1895-1986), the Irish writer on Advaita, Ch'an and Taoism. The line is stylistically and doctrinally characteristic of his aphoristic books of the 1960s, and I know of no competing attribution. I cannot place the exact volume or page from training knowledge - candidates are 'Ask the Awakened: The Negative Way' (1963) and 'All Else Is Bondage: Non-Volitional Living' (1964) - so I leave the print source null rather than guess. Author attribution strong; citation unlocated.

Back to purity, back to simplicity.' The principles are documented by Vitsoe and reproduced in the Rams literature (e.g. 'Weniger, aber besser / Less but Better', 1995). Attribution is not in doubt.

Very widely and consistently attributed to Gandhi, and consonant with his writing on ahimsa, but I cannot place it in a specific issue of Young India, Harijan, or the Collected Works from training knowledge. Gandhi is a major misattribution magnet, so I hold this below the promotion bar until someone can point to a dated original. Attribution plausible and uncontested; citation unlocated.

Genuinely Mother Teresa's sentiment, expressed many times in slightly different words; the most commonly documented form is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' The wording here is a widespread variant that appears in the posthumous compilations (e.g. 'A Simple Path', 1995; 'The Joy in Loving'). Because she repeated the thought in varying phrasings and I cannot fix this exact sentence to a dated text, I keep it just below the bar.

Verifiable by anyone with the book; treat as unconfirmed until then.

Not a misattribution to a different author, so no reattribution offered.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter from Birmingham Jail, Martin Luther King, Jr., 16 April 1963
