As solid a provenance as this corpus will contain.

No French original in Voltaire's works corresponds to this line as far as I know, and it circulates almost exclusively in English aphorism collections and on quote sites without a citation. Voltaire is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus of freethought quotations (the fabricated 'I disapprove of what you say...' line being the classic case). The related genuine sentiment usually cited is Goethe's 'None are more hopelessly enslaved than those who falsely believe they are free,' which is a different quote. I have no defensible true origin, so no reattribution. Recommend rejection or a clear 'attributed to' hedge.

results.earliest_print_source: Speech in Selma, Alabama, 8 March 1965
results.notes: Authentic King, generally sourced to his remarks in Selma on 8 March 1965 (the day after Bloody Sunday), which is the citation carried on Wikiquote and in King anthologies. My confidence in the King attribution is high; my confidence in that exact date and occasion is good but not certain, which is why I stop short of verified.

results.earliest_print_source: Strength to Love, Martin Luther King, Jr., 1963 (sermon 'Loving Your Enemies')
results.notes: Authentic King, from the 'Loving Your Enemies' sermon collected in 'Strength to Love' (1963). One wording caution: King's published sentence ends 'plunged into the dark abyss of annihilation,' not 'the darkness of annihilation,' and the passage here is a condensation joining sentences separated in the original by the ellipsis. Recommend restoring the published wording. Attribution itself is beyond doubt.

results.earliest_print_source: 'I've Been to the Mountaintop', Mason Temple, Memphis, 3 April 1968
results.notes: King said this in his final speech, 'I've Been to the Mountaintop,' the night before his assassination: 'Only when it is dark enough can you see the stars.' Worth noting for the corpus that King was invoking an older aphorism, commonly credited to the historian Charles A. Beard and sometimes loosely to Emerson; King is the popularizer rather than the originator of the thought, but the utterance attributed to him is genuine.

I cannot locate this sentence in Wilde's plays, essays, letters, or the 'Phrases and Philosophies for the Use of the Young.' It reads like a compression of two documented Wilde lines: 'Life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it' (Lady Windermere's Fan, 1892; also in Vera) and 'We should treat all the trivial things of life seriously, and all the serious things of life with sincere and studied triviality.' Wilde attracts unsourced epigrams the way Twain attracts folksy ones. Also frequently confused with Niels Bohr's 'There are some things so serious you have to laugh at them.' No confident true origin, so no reattribution.

The pre-flag is correct. This appears in no Einstein primary source and is absent from Alice Calaprice's 'The Ultimate Quotable Einstein,' the standard scholarly filter; documented instances begin decades after Einstein's 1955 death, in late-twentieth-century business, advertising, and creativity literature. Quote investigators have pointed at a modern advertising/creativity author (I recall Joey Reiman being named) as an early user rather than Einstein, but my recollection of that trail is not firm enough to assert a reattribution, so I leave the field null. Recommend rejection or relabeling as anonymous.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter of condolence to the family of Michele Besso, 21 March 1955 (published in the Einstein-Besso correspondence; quoted in 'Einstein: The Human Side')
results.notes: Unlike most 'Einstein' aphorisms this one has a real root: writing to Michele Besso's family weeks before his own death, Einstein wrote that for believing physicists 'the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubborn persistent illusion.' The version in the corpus is a loose paraphrase - it pluralizes 'illusions' and drops the crucial framing 'for us believing physicists,' which changes the claim from a remark about physics to a metaphysical assertion. Attribution to Einstein is genuine; this wording is not his. Strongly recommend replacing with the accurate translation, after which it would merit verified status.

results.earliest_print_source: Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham, Agnes de Mille, 1991
results.notes: Authentically Agnes de Mille and consistently attributed to her; the passage is the well-known one whose elided middle reads 'The moment you know how, you begin to die a little.' It is usually cited to her Graham biography 'Martha: The Life and Work of Martha Graham' (1991), the same book that carries the famous Graham 'divine dissatisfaction' passage, and I believe that citation is right but cannot confirm the page. No competing attribution.

The idea is genuinely Rogers's, but this four-word form is not his wording. In 'On Becoming a Person' (1961), in the chapter 'This Is Me,' he writes 'what is most personal is most general.' The variant 'what is most personal is most universal' circulates widely and is sometimes attributed to Rogers directly, sometimes to later writers restating him. 'The personal is the universal' is a further compression by an unknown hand and may also be blending with the second-wave feminist slogan 'the personal is political' (Carol Hanisch, 1969). Recommend replacing with the sourced 1961 sentence.

results.earliest_print_source: Music at Night and Other Essays, Aldous Huxley, 1931 (essay 'The Rest Is Silence')
results.notes: Genuine Huxley, from 'Music at Night and Other Essays' (1931), in the essay 'The Rest Is Silence.' The sentence circulates verbatim and matches the published text. One of the reliably sourced quotations in this batch.

Alan Cohen is a real inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart) and this line circulates consistently under his name on quote sites and in daily-inspiration compilations. I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or dated column from training knowledge, and Cohen's aphorisms are almost always recirculated without citation. The attribution is plausible and uncontested but unsourced.

Consistently attributed to Gandhi across collections, and the ocean/drops image is idiomatically consistent with his writing in Young India and Harijan. However, I cannot locate a primary source — no specific issue, speech, or volume of the Collected Works comes to mind, and I do not know whether this sits in the sourced or the unsourced section of Gandhi's Wikiquote page. Gandhi is a heavy misattribution magnet, so consistent repetition is not itself evidence. Honest verdict: plausibly genuine, unverified.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Gandhi source for this; it does not appear in the Collected Works so far as I know, and it is generally listed among Gandhi's misattributed lines. The saying is far older than Gandhi: a closely matching maxim ('Study as if you were to live forever; live as if you were to die tomorrow') is traditionally ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon, the 13th-century Archbishop of Canterbury, and circulated in English proverb collections well before Gandhi's lifetime. The James Dean attribution is a separate later graft and is also unsupported. I am confident it is not Gandhi's; I am only moderately confident in the Edmund of Abingdon lineage, which is itself a tradition rather than a documented autograph.
results.suggested_reattribution: Traditional maxim long ascribed to St. Edmund of Abingdon (13th c.); not Gandhi

results.earliest_print_source: Statement to Christian Zervos, 'Conversation avec Picasso,' Cahiers d'Art, 1935
results.notes: This belongs to Picasso's well-known 1935 statement recorded by Christian Zervos and published in Cahiers d'Art, the same conversation that produced 'a picture is not thought out and settled beforehand.' The English rendering circulating today comes from the translation reprinted in Alfred H. Barr Jr.'s Picasso monograph and in Herschel B. Chipp's Theories of Modern Art (1968). I am confident about the 1935 Zervos conversation as the origin but have not pinned the exact page in the translated reprints, so I am holding just under the promotion bar rather than claiming primary verification.

Idiomatically very close to Watts's recurring theme that naming and classifying substitute for direct perception (developed at length in The Wisdom of Insecurity and The Book), but I cannot place this exact sentence in any Watts book or transcribed lecture. Watts's recorded talks are a large, loosely transcribed corpus, which makes attractive one-liners easy to attach to him without evidence. Plausible but unsourced.

The thought is authentically Jungian — it matches his insistence that the psyche is not contained inside the skull ('we are in the psyche' rather than the psyche being in us) and his late work on synchronicity and the unus mundus. But I cannot locate this exact sentence in the Collected Works, the letters, or Memories, Dreams, Reflections. Jung is frequently paraphrased into crisper English than he wrote, and this reads like such a condensation. Unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Most Durable Power,' Martin Luther King Jr., The Christian Century, 1957 (from a sermon delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, November 1956)
results.notes: This is King's own language from the sermon/essay 'The Most Durable Power,' delivered at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church during the closing weeks of the Montgomery bus boycott and excerpted in The Christian Century in 1957; it is indexed in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr. and reprinted in A Testament of Hope. The wording here (durable power / creative force / exemplified in the life of our Christ / quest for peace and security) matches the published text. I am confident in the sermon and the Christian Century publication; I am not certain of the exact issue date, so treat the year rather than a day as the firm part of the citation.

results.earliest_print_source: 'What I Believe,' Albert Einstein, Forum and Century, vol. 84, 1930; collected in The World As I See It, 1931 (Mein Weltbild, 1934)
results.notes: Genuine Einstein, and unusually well documented for him. This is the closing passage of his credo essay 'What I Believe,' published in Forum and Century in 1930 and collected in The World As I See It. The long form quoted here matches the standard English translation, including 'as good as dead; his eyes are closed' and the concluding 'this knowledge, this feeling is at the center of true religiousness.' Truncated one-line versions circulate widely, but the full passage given here is faithful.

The pre-flag is correct. There is no Einstein source for this, in his published papers, essays, letters, or the standard quotation references. It reads as a design-industry aphorism of recent vintage, most likely a loose descendant of the genuine Einstein simplicity theme (see q_0180) that acquired his name for authority. I cannot identify a real originator, so 'apocryphal' rather than 'likely_misattributed' — I have no probable true author to offer, and inventing one would be worse than admitting that.

results.earliest_print_source: Roger Sessions, 'How a Difficult Composer Gets That Way,' The New York Times, January 8, 1950
results.notes: The idea is Einstein's; the epigram is not his wording. Einstein's documented statement is from the 1933 Herbert Spencer Lecture 'On the Method of Theoretical Physics': the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without surrendering the adequate representation of a single datum of experience. The compact form entered print when the composer Roger Sessions reported it secondhand in the New York Times in 1950 — explicitly as a remark Einstein made 'in effect,' i.e. Sessions's own condensation. Everything since descends from that paraphrase. Genuine sentiment, secondhand phrasing; deliberately held below the promotion bar because the corpus would be presenting a paraphrase as Einstein's words.

results.earliest_print_source: Richard L. Evans's Quote Book, 1971 (crediting Carl W. Buehner)
results.notes: The pre-flag is right to hedge. Angelou did use versions of this in interviews and talks from the 1990s onward, so the attribution is not fabricated — but the aphorism predates her. The earliest known instance credits Carl W. Buehner: 'They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel,' printed in Richard L. Evans's Quote Book (1971). Angelou's characteristic triad ('what you said / what you did / how you made them feel') is her expansion of an existing saying, and I cannot fix a first Angelou utterance or its exact wording. Safest handling: treat the wording as unverified and do not present it as an original Angelou line.

Definitely not Lincoln — nothing like it appears in the Collected Works, and the managerial idiom is anachronistic for the 1860s; it is a standard Lincoln graft. The Drucker attribution in the author field is the common replacement but is itself weakly evidenced: I cannot point to the book or article where Drucker wrote it. The best-documented neighbor is Alan Kay's 'The best way to predict the future is to invent it' (Xerox PARC, early 1970s), and Dennis Gabor's Inventing the Future (1963) argues that the future cannot be predicted but can be invented. The 'create it' variant floats between Drucker, Kay, Gabor, and Forrest Shaklee. Since I cannot say which is right, no reattribution.

Consistently and, as far as I know, uncontestedly attributed to the American essayist Agnes Repplier (1855-1950), and the epigrammatic balance is characteristic of her prose. It is usually cited to one of her essay collections — Compromises (1904) is the volume most often named — but I cannot confirm the volume or essay from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Attribution is stable; the citation is not established.

Same situation as q_0166. Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever it appears and consistent with his register, but recirculated without citation and not placeable in a specific book or column from training knowledge. Uncontested but unsourced.

As with the other two Alan Cohen entries in this batch: plausible, uncontested, and unsourced. I cannot place it in a titled work, and Cohen's material circulates chiefly through daily-inspiration excerpts that drop citations.

Strongly Wattsian in both idea and vocabulary — 'aperture' is a word he genuinely used for the individual as the universe's point of self-awareness, and the thought parallels the documented passages in The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) about the universe peopling and looking at itself through our eyes. I cannot confirm this exact sentence in a printed Watts text, and much of the Watts material online comes from loosely transcribed lectures. Likely genuine in substance, wording unverified.

One of the most widely reproduced Watts lines, attributed to him with unusual consistency and squarely on the theme of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is the book most often cited for it. I cannot confirm the page or even the volume from memory, so I am not recording a print source. The stability of the attribution earns 'attributed,' but without a located passage it stays below the promotion bar.

No primary source. This is one of the modest-genius lines that accrete to Einstein, and I cannot trace it to a paper, letter, or documented interview. The genuine, well-sourced neighbor is his letter to Carl Seelig of 11 March 1952: 'I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.' The 'stay with problems longer' phrasing looks like a later restatement of that sentiment rather than something Einstein wrote. Uncertain, and Einstein's misattribution record argues for caution.

No Einstein source exists for this; it is routinely listed among his misattributed quotations. The phrasing is late-20th/21st-century motivational English and has the shape of a slogan retrofitted with a famous name — it may owe something to popularized readings of adaptability in intelligence research, but I know of no real originator and will not guess one. Recommend it not be promoted under Einstein's name in any form.

results.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Text, Chapter 21, Introduction (T-21.in.1), Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976
results.notes: Genuine and locatable. This is the opening of Chapter 21 of the ACIM Text ('Reason and Perception'), which begins 'Projection makes perception' and continues through 'Therefore, seek not to change the world, but choose to change your mind about the world.' The second sentence quoted here ('What you see reflects your thinking...') is from the same introductory passage. Wording matches the Foundation for Inner Peace edition. Note the source is a work, not a person — the corpus should credit A Course in Miracles rather than Helen Schucman personally, which matches the input.

The sentence matches ACIM's definition of the ego as the mind's belief in its own separation and autonomy, and it is quoted as ACIM in the secondary literature around the Course (Wapnick and others). I cannot pin the chapter and section, and ACIM circulates in multiple editions with different numbering, so I am not recording a citation I cannot place. Very likely genuine to the work; location unconfirmed.

Reads as authentic ACIM in cadence and doctrine (freedom of belief, and behavior as the witness to belief), and it is quoted as such, but I cannot locate the passage in the Text, Workbook, or Manual for Teachers from memory. Slightly lower confidence than q_0191 because I have less independent recall of this specific line. Genuine-looking but unlocated.

Extremely widely attributed to Helen Keller and not, to my knowledge, contested or reassigned to anyone else — but I cannot trace it to a book, essay, letter, or speech of hers. It is a staple of teamwork posters and fundraising copy, which is exactly the environment in which citations disappear. Plausible; unsourced.

results.earliest_print_source: Robert G. Ingersoll, lecture 'Abraham Lincoln,' 1883
results.notes: Not Lincoln. Nothing of the kind appears in the Collected Works, and the attribution is 20th-century. The near-certain origin is Robert G. Ingersoll's celebrated lecture on Lincoln (1883), which argues: 'Nothing discloses real character like the use of power... Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is, give him power.' A statement made *about* Lincoln was over time converted into a statement *by* Lincoln — a common mechanism for this particular magnet. Confidence value reflects the weakness of the Lincoln attribution; my confidence in the Ingersoll origin is considerably higher.
results.suggested_reattribution: Robert G. Ingersoll, from his 1883 lecture on Abraham Lincoln

results.earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
results.notes: The thought is documented Maslow: Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) frames growth as a repeated choice, in the form 'one can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth,' with growth chosen over and over and fear overcome again and again. The wording quoted here ('You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety') is the popular circulating variant rather than the printed sentence I can attest to, and it is often given in the second person as if from a lecture. Substance verified in the 1962 book; exact wording is a variant, so it should be presented as Maslow's idea, ideally with the printed phrasing substituted.

results.earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
results.notes: This is Maslow's core safety-versus-growth dialectic, which he develops explicitly in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), especially the 'Defense and Growth' material where he frames each moment as a choice between the delights/anxieties of safety and those of growth. The line is consistently attributed to that book across psychology literature and I recall it as Maslow's own phrasing rather than a paraphrase. I cannot confirm a page number from memory, so this is strong secondary rather than page-verified.

Abraham-Hicks material is channeled workshop transcript published by Esther and Jerry Hicks; individual passages circulate with a workshop city and date on the official site and in the Daily Quote mailings. The vocabulary and cadence here (the abundance 'flowing in many more avenues than dollars', 'delicious people', the recursive stacking of 'the abundance of...') is highly characteristic of the Abraham corpus, so authorship is plausible. But I cannot place this passage in a specific workshop, recording, or book, and transcript excerpts are routinely re-cut and paraphrased by quote sites. Attribution to the source is plausible; the exact wording is unverified.

Alan Cohen is a real and prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart, Enough Already), and this line is consistent with his aphoristic voice and his recurring 'the treasure is within you' theme. However, I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or newsletter. His one-liners circulate almost entirely through quote aggregators and his own daily-inspiration mailings, which leaves no verifiable print chain. Honest verdict: plausible author, no evidence.

This longer passage ('we are divinely created love machines', well-being depends on giving rather than receiving love) reads as genuine Alan Cohen prose rather than a quote-site fragment — the paragraph structure and the gentle contrarian turn are his. I have a weak recollection of this theme in his book-length work but cannot name the title or year with any confidence, and I will not guess one. Attribution plausible, source unlocated.

Consistent with Alan Cohen's writing on self-care and the helper's blind spot, and widely reproduced under his name. No specific book, article, or dated newsletter can be identified from my training knowledge, and no primary text is available to confirm the wording. Plausible but unevidenced.

Attributed to Alan Cohen across quote sites and thematically of a piece with q_0198 (greatness is internal, not imported). Note the transmitted text is ungrammatical — 'is turn your back' is missing 'to', which is a signature of quote-aggregator copying rather than a book text, and suggests the wording here has drifted from whatever the original was. No source located; no independent evidence for the attribution.

The 'watch what follows I AM' teaching is a shared commonplace of New Thought and metaphysical writing (Emmet Fox, Florence Scovel Shinn, Wayne Dyer, Joel Goldsmith and many others all state versions of it), so this particular phrasing is not distinctive enough for me to assign it to Alan Cohen on internal evidence. He may well have written it; the idea is not original to him. No source located.

This is a variant of the widely circulated 'Imagination is everything. It is the preview of life's coming attractions,' which is popularly attributed to Albert Einstein and has no basis in his writings — it is a well-known apocryphal Einstein line. The 'coming attractions' movie-trailer metaphor therefore has muddled provenance predating any Cohen usage, and the same sentence also floats attributed to Louise Hay and others. Alan Cohen may have used this phrasing, but the attribution chain is contaminated. Low confidence in the recorded author; I cannot identify who coined the movie-trailer formulation.

Gratitude-versus-complaint framing stated as a ratio; consistent with Alan Cohen's aphoristic style and widely reproduced under his name. No book, article, or dated source identifiable from training knowledge.

A reworking of the older idiom 'waiting for my ship to come in' (which is a proverbial commonplace, not anyone's coinage) and close in shape to several circulating variants such as 'Don't wait for your ship to come in — swim out to it' and 'your ship has already come in.' The specific inversion here is attributed to Alan Cohen on quote sites, but the idiom's ubiquity makes independent coinage likely in multiple mouths. No source located.

Reads like an instruction from a practice-oriented passage or daily-inspiration entry, which matches how most Alan Cohen quotations enter circulation. Plausibly his; no specific book, chapter, or dated mailing identifiable, and no independent corroboration of the attribution.

The construction ('radiate wholeness, a rare delicacy in a world of hungry hearts') is more crafted than the average aggregator one-liner and is idiomatic of Alan Cohen's prose, which raises my confidence that it is genuinely his and not a floating anonymous line. I still cannot place it in a specific title — his books on people-pleasing and contentment are the likeliest home but I will not name one as a citation without being able to confirm it.

Attributed to Alan Cohen and consistent with his voice and his frequent play on conventional life-stage language. No primary source identifiable; the only visible provenance is quote-aggregator repetition, which is not evidence.

results.earliest_print_source: Nature, Man and Woman, Alan Watts, 1958
results.notes: Genuine Alan Watts, and unusually well sourced for him: this passage is consistently cited to Nature, Man and Woman (1958), and I recall it appearing in the sourced (not the 'attributed') portion of his Wikiquote entry. The argument — that purposiveness makes the senses miss the world, and that purposelessness is receptive — is a central thesis of that book, and the extended paragraph form is authentic Watts prose rather than a lecture-transcript fragment. Marked attributed rather than verified only because I cannot confirm the page from memory.

Authentically Watts in both idea and image. The self-referential-impossibility metaphor is one he used repeatedly in variant forms — biting your own teeth, seeing your own eyes, lifting yourself by your own bootstraps, the knife that cannot cut itself — deployed against the notion of a self that can stand outside itself and define itself. The attribution to Watts is strong on internal evidence and consistent citation. I cannot pin it to a particular book or lecture, however; many circulating Watts lines come from recorded talks that were later transcribed, so no print source is offered.

results.earliest_print_source: "Retour à Tipasa", in L'Été, Albert Camus, 1954 (essay first published 1952)
results.notes: Genuine Camus, from the essay 'Retour à Tipasa' ('Return to Tipasa'), collected in L'Été (Summer, 1954). Original French: 'Au milieu de l'hiver, j'apprenais enfin qu'il y avait en moi un été invincible.' Note the English here is the loose popular rendering; a closer translation is 'In the midst of winter, I finally learned that there was in me an invincible summer.' The substitution of 'I found' for 'I learned at last' and the stray comma before 'an invincible summer' are artifacts of quote-site transmission, so the attribution is verified but the wording is a paraphrase of the standard translation.

results.earliest_print_source: The Fall (La Chute), Albert Camus, 1956, trans. Justin O'Brien
results.notes: From The Fall (La Chute, 1956), spoken by the narrator Jean-Baptiste Clamence in his monologue about the pleasures of his earlier life. The diction ('to sooth one another mutually', 'condemn such joys as selfishness') is the Justin O'Brien English translation. Important context for corpus use: this is a fictional character's self-justifying confession, not Camus speaking in his own voice — Clamence is an unreliable narrator and the novel is an indictment of exactly this posture. Attribution to Camus as author is sound; presenting it as Camus's personal counsel would misread it.

One of the most-repeated Einstein lines and not found in his writings in this form. What Einstein actually said is documented: in a May 1946 telegram from the Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists, quoted in the New York Times, 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive and move toward higher levels.' The popular 'we cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them' is a much later compression, appearing in management and self-help literature decades afterward, and it is treated as unsourced in the Einstein quotation scholarship (Calaprice's collections place this family of sayings outside the verified material). Kept as attributed_unverified rather than apocryphal because a genuine Einstein statement sits at the root of the paraphrase — but the sentence as written should not be quoted as his words.

No evidence Einstein said or wrote this; it is a standard entry in the misattributed-Einstein lists and does not appear in his published papers, letters, or interviews. The nearest documented ancestor belongs to Ernest Rutherford, reported as saying that a physical theory is no good unless you can explain it to a barmaid — a remark recorded secondhand and itself imperfectly sourced. Similar sentiments are also attributed to Feynman. The Einstein version appears to be a late-twentieth-century construction with no traceable origin, so no true author can be named.

Circulated as Einstein's 'Three Rules of Work.' No primary source exists — it does not appear in his papers or correspondence, and the triad structure is characteristic of twentieth-century motivational compilation rather than of Einstein's prose. The third clause, 'in the middle of difficulty lies opportunity,' is the oldest and most widely repeated of the three and appears in Einstein quotation collections under attributed-but-unsourced headings; even that one has no located primary text. Treat the whole triad as unverified.

A well-documented misattribution, usually circulated in the longer form beginning 'Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree...'. It appears nowhere in Einstein's writings and is absent from the scholarly Einstein quotation collections; researchers tracing it have found no instance in his lifetime, with the saying surfacing in this shape only in recent decades. The same pedagogical point is made in George Reavis's fable 'The Animal School' (circulated from around 1940), which is a thematic analogue rather than a demonstrated source. No credible author can be identified.

Attributed to Alan Cohen and compatible with his relationship writing, but this is a generic self-help formulation ('X is not something that happens to you, it is something you choose') that recurs verbatim in many authors' work about love, happiness, and success. The template is too common for the wording alone to establish authorship, and no source can be located.

The recorded author appears to be a confusion of two different Dutch writers. My recollection places this line with J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw, 1893-1934), the Dutch theosophical writer, in his book The Conquest of Illusion (1928), whose opening pages frame life as a mystery to be lived rather than a problem to be solved. Aart van der Leeuw (1876-1931) was a separate Dutch poet and novelist, and the surname collision is the likely origin of the swap. The quote is also frequently and wrongly attributed to Frank Herbert via Dune, and to various others, which shows how loose its circulation is. I hold the J.J. van der Leeuw reattribution at moderate confidence only — the confidence value given reflects the weak standing of the recorded 'Aart' attribution. Do not promote without checking the 1928 text.
results.suggested_reattribution: J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw), The Conquest of Illusion (1928) — moderate confidence, needs confirmation against the text

results.notes: The imagery ('dismal dream of limitation', 'the eagle of your sacred visions') is distinctly Alan Cohen's devotional register and closely echoes the A Course in Miracles vocabulary he works within, which supports his authorship. Still no locatable book, chapter, or dated source; his aphorisms of this kind typically originate in daily-inspiration mailings that leave no citable print record.

Sounds authentically like Alan Watts speaking rather than writing — the clipped fragments and the spoken-register repetition are typical of his recorded lectures, and the point (that 'you' and 'I' are shared pronouns naming the same universal subject) is one he made often. But precisely because it reads as transcript, I cannot tie it to a specific talk, recording, or published text, and lecture transcriptions of Watts circulate in many loosely edited versions. Plausibly genuine, wording unverified.

The line reads like a translation of Camus ('j'etais absent au moment ou je prenais le plus de place') and is thematically consistent with the self-accusing narrator of La Chute (The Fall, 1956) or the Carnets. I cannot place it in a specific work or confirm the translation, and I will not name a book I am not sure of. Attribution to Camus is plausible and consistently made, but unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Farewell Address at Springfield, Illinois, February 11, 1861; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. IV
results.notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the Springfield farewell remarks delivered on departing for Washington. The documented wording is 'Without the assistance of that Divine Being, who ever attended him, I cannot succeed. With that assistance I cannot fail.' The corpus text is a lightly trimmed version of that sentence; the substance and the source event are secure.

A very widely repeated Lincoln line, but it rests on later recollection rather than a contemporaneous document. It circulates via post-assassination memoirs and religious biographies of Lincoln, and reference works generally file it under attributed rather than sourced. Lincoln is a known misattribution magnet, so I am holding this below the promotion bar; the sentiment fits his recorded remarks about religion, but no primary source is in my knowledge.

'Adept Godrakpa' is the distinctive rendering used for Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje (1189-1258), the Tibetan Kagyu yogi, in Cyrus Stearns' translation of his songs of realization published by Wisdom Publications around 2000. The imagery (body like spring mist, mind like empty sky, thoughts like breezes) and the three-point contemplative structure match that body of doggerel-song instruction closely, so the attribution is probably right. I am not certain enough of the exact page or the exact translated wording to record a print citation, so the source field stays null.

Alan Cohen is a prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, Wisdom of the Heart) whose aphorisms circulate through books, newsletters, and daily-quote services with consistent attribution but almost never with a book-and-page citation. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; no primary source in my knowledge.

Same situation as the other Alan Cohen aphorisms in this batch: consistently attributed to him across quote collections, no traceable first appearance in my knowledge. Nothing suggests a different author; the uncertainty is about sourcing, not about who wrote it.

Widely circulated as Alan Cohen, typically without citation. The left-brain/right-brain framing places it in the late-twentieth-century self-help idiom he writes in, which is consistent with the attribution, but I cannot locate a specific book or column.

Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever I have seen it, with no source given. Short enough and aphoristic enough that provenance drift is easy; I have no evidence of an earlier or different author, but no evidence for the attribution beyond repetition either.

Attributed to Alan Cohen without citation. Worth flagging that the idea, and nearly the phrasing, is central to Anthony de Mello's Awareness ('spirituality means waking up... most people are asleep and don't know it'), so this may be a restatement of de Mello that acquired Cohen's name, or a genuine Cohen line in the same lineage. I cannot tell which, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

Consistently attributed to Alan Cohen and one of his more frequently reproduced lines, which slightly strengthens the attribution, but I can point to no book, essay, or dated appearance. Sourcing unverified.
Attributed to Alan Cohen in quote collections with no citation. Voice and vocabulary are consistent with his other work; nothing more than that supports it.

This is a Buddhist scriptural formula, not an Alan Watts original. The line 'Things are not what they seem, nor are they otherwise' is a well-known rendering from the Lankavatara Sutra, and Watts quoted this kind of formulation in his writing on Zen and Mahayana. Attributing it to Watts credits the popularizer rather than the source. My confidence is in the Lankavatara provenance of the formula; I cannot confirm which translation this exact English wording comes from, and it is possible Watts's own paraphrase is what circulates.
results.suggested_reattribution: Lankavatara Sutra (as quoted/paraphrased by Alan Watts)

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Isham Reavis, November 5, 1855; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. II
results.notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the letter of advice to Isham Reavis, a young man who had asked about studying law. The documented wording is 'Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing'; the corpus text drops 'other'. I am confident about the letter and the recipient; consider restoring the original wording.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Principles of Research', address at Max Planck's 60th birthday celebration, Physical Society, Berlin, 1918; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: Authentic Einstein from the 1918 Planck birthday address, one of his best-documented statements about how physical theory is actually arrived at. Original reads 'no logical way to the discovery of these elemental laws'; the corpus text drops 'these'. Source and occasion are secure.

I cannot place this in Alan Watts's books or recorded talks. The idea (a mind in its natural state, unfixed and therefore able to respond in any direction) is standard mushin/wu-hsin material that Watts wrote about in The Way of Zen, and the phrasing also resembles English renderings of Takuan Soho's The Unfettered Mind, which Watts drew on. That makes the attribution plausible but unsupported. Possibly a paraphrase of Watts rather than his words.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or interviews that I know of; reference compilations of Einstein quotations treat it as attributed rather than sourced. The sentiment closely tracks a documented Niels Bohr remark to Wolfgang Pauli ('we are all agreed that your theory is crazy; the question is whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct'), and this may be a compressed folk version of that exchange re-badged with Einstein's name. I cannot establish the true origin, so no reattribution.

This reads as authentic Einstein prose and I recall it from collections of his writings on the religious feeling of the scientist, associated with his early-1930s credo material ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis' / The World As I See It). The distinctive cadence and the 'neither evolution nor eternity, only being' close are hard to fake and are consistent with his German essays in translation. I am confident enough in authorship to call it attributed, but I cannot pin the exact essay or year, so I am leaving the citation null and staying under the promotion bar.

I have no record of this in Einstein's writings, and it sits awkwardly against his documented positions, which consistently favour inquiry over belief and reject the 'better to believe' framing as such. It circulates mainly through quotation websites. Einstein is the single largest misattribution magnet in the corpus; absent any source, this should not be promoted.

I believe this is authentic Einstein, from his mid-1930s statements collected in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild, and it is quoted with consistent wording in serious Einstein compilations rather than only on quote sites. The phrase 'love and devotion towards men and towards objective things' is a characteristic translation of his German. I cannot confirm the specific essay or letter, so the citation stays null and I am holding below 0.80.

Authentic Einstein as far as I know it. The fuller passage continues 'It cannot lead, it can only serve; and it is not fastidious in its choice of a leader', and it appears in the standard English collections of his essays (Ideas and Opinions / Out of My Later Years). The extended, coherent context is good evidence of genuineness. I am not certain enough which original essay or year it comes from to record an earliest print source, so it sits just under the promotion bar pending a human check against Ideas and Opinions.

Almost certainly a paraphrase rather than Einstein's words. What is documented is his 1946 campaign for atomic-age rethinking: 'The unleashed power of the atom has changed everything save our modes of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparalleled catastrophe', and 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive'. This line compresses that into modern self-help phrasing. No source for this exact wording. Closely related to q_0243 below, which is the better-known version of the same drift.

One of the most-repeated Einstein misattributions and a documented case of quote drift. It has no source in Einstein's writings; the wording appears in late-twentieth-century management, therapy, and self-help literature and was retro-attributed to him, evolving out of his genuine 1946 remarks about needing a new mode of thinking in the atomic age. Quote-investigation work and the standard Einstein quotation reference both place it in the unsourced/misattributed category. No identifiable individual author, so apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

I am fairly confident this is authentic. The German original is known ('Wer sich als Richter auf dem Gebiete der Wahrheit und Erkenntnis aufzuwerfen unternimmt, wird vom Gelaechter der Goetter zerschmettert'), which is strong evidence against a modern English-language invention, and it is generally dated to an Einstein aphorism of the early 1950s. I cannot confirm the publication it first appeared in, so no citation and no promotion; a human check against the standard Einstein quotation reference should settle it.

Consistently attributed to Einstein and compatible with his documented views on social obligation ('a hundred times every day I remind myself that my inner and outer life are based on the labors of other men'), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings or interviews. The plain, proverbial phrasing is the kind that attracts famous names. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

Correctly pre-flagged. There is no Einstein source for this; it does not appear in his published writings, letters, or interviews, and the standard Einstein quotation reference lists it among sayings attributed to him without support. Attributions to Einstein surface long after his death and appear to be a rebadging of an older inspirational commonplace. No identifiable original author, so apocryphal.

results.earliest_print_source: Relativity: The Special and the General Theory, Albert Einstein, 1916 (German); English translation 1920, Chapter VII
results.notes: This is the opening sentence of Chapter VII ('The Apparent Incompatibility of the Law of Propagation of Light with the Principle of Relativity') of Einstein's own popular exposition Relativity: The Special and the General Theory. Einstein wrote the book himself, so this is a primary source in his own words rather than a reported remark. Wording matches the standard Robert W. Lawson English translation.

Consistently attributed to Einstein and entirely consonant with his documented pacifist writings of the late 1920s and 1930s, where the force-versus-understanding contrast recurs. I cannot place the specific document from memory — candidates I associate with it (a c. 1930 pacifist statement, the material collected in Mein Weltbild / The World As I See It, or the Einstein on Peace compilation) are recollections I am not confident enough to print as a citation, so I have left the source field null rather than guess. Kept below the promotion bar for that reason.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Geometrie und Erfahrung' ('Geometry and Experience'), address to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, Berlin, 27 January 1921
results.notes: One of the best-documented Einstein lines. Delivered in his 1921 Prussian Academy address on geometry and experience and reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954). The corpus text drops the semicolon-and joining the two clauses but is otherwise the standard translation.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or recorded conversations. This is a stock item in the unsourced/misattributed section of the Einstein Wikiquote page. It surfaces in motivational compilations decades after his death and reads as a modern aphorism rather than a translation from German. It is likely a compressed echo of his genuine 'Imagination is more important than knowledge' (Viereck interview, 1929), but the 'A to B' phrasing is not his. I cannot identify who actually coined it.

Heavily circulated in vegetarian advocacy literature but not found in Einstein's collected writings or correspondence; it appears in the misattributed material on the Einstein Wikiquote page. Einstein's authentic statements on the subject are different and much more qualified — the 1930 letter to Hermann Huth ('Although I have been prevented by outward circumstances from observing a strictly vegetarian diet, I have long been an adherent to the cause in principle') and a 1954 letter to Hans Muehsam written after he adopted the diet on medical advice. The sweeping 'survival of life on Earth' framing is not his idiom. True coiner unknown to me.

Very widely attributed, including in education scholarship, and a German original circulates ('Es ist die wichtigste Kunst des Lehrers, die Freude am Schaffen und Erkennen zu wecken'), which is mild evidence of genuine provenance rather than a back-translated invention. But I cannot place a primary document. It is plausibly connected to his writings and addresses on education (e.g. the 1936 Albany address 'On Education'), yet I do not actually recall it in that text, and some Einstein quote scholarship files lines of this kind as unsourced. Honest verdict: probably his, not demonstrable from what I know.

The joke is authentically Einstein's — it was his stock popular gloss on relativity, given to reporters (his secretary Helen Dukas handed out a version of it) and recorded in multiple accounts from the late 1920s onward. Two cautions. First, this specific wording ('courting a nice girl', 'red-hot cinder') is one of several circulating variants; the more commonly documented form is 'When you sit with a nice girl for two hours it seems like a minute; when you sit on a hot stove for a minute it seems like two hours.' Second, the citation often attached to it online — 'Journal of Exothermic Science and Technology (JEST), Vol. 1, No. 9, 1938' — is a spoof, not a real journal, so I have deliberately not printed it. Substance solid, exact wording and source not verifiable.

results.earliest_print_source: 'The Common Language of Science', radio address recorded for the British Association for the Advancement of Science, 28 September 1941; reprinted in Out of My Later Years (1950) and Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: This is the closing sentence of Einstein's short 1941 broadcast on the common language of science. Written by Einstein for delivery, so a primary source. Corpus text matches the standard printed version including the parenthetical dashes.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Morris Raphael Cohen, 19 March 1940, written in support of Bertrand Russell's appointment at the College of the City of New York
results.notes: Genuine and well documented. Einstein wrote it to philosopher Morris Raphael Cohen during the public campaign against Russell's teaching appointment. Despite being a heavily meme-ified line, this one survives scrutiny — the letter is real and the context is specific.

results.earliest_print_source: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered, E. F. Schumacher, 1973
results.notes: I do not believe this is Einstein's. I recall it from E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973), where the wording runs 'Any intelligent fool can make things bigger, more complex, and more violent. It takes a touch of genius — and a lot of courage — to move in the opposite direction.' Note that the corpus version has dropped 'intelligent', which is the tell of a quote that has passed through attribution drift. Caveat on my own certainty: I am confident the line is Schumacher's in print and not Einstein's, but less certain whether Schumacher coined it or was himself echoing an earlier source, so treat the reattribution as probable rather than settled.
results.suggested_reattribution: E. F. Schumacher

results.earliest_print_source: Esther Salaman, 'A Talk With Einstein', The Listener, vol. 54 (1955)
results.notes: This is a compression of a longer remark Einstein made to the physicist Esther Salaman around 1925, which she published from memory in 1955: 'I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon, in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details.' So the source is a recollection recorded roughly thirty years after the conversation, and the popular one-sentence form here is an editor's condensation rather than Einstein's own sentence. Genuine in substance; the exact wording is not.

results.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck, 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929 (republished in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
results.notes: I recall this from the 1929 Viereck interview, the same conversation that produced 'Imagination is more important than knowledge.' The 'gift of fantasy' phrasing is characteristic of that interview's translation. Hedge: I am confident about the interview but not about the exact page, and I cannot rule out that the line comes from a neighbouring Viereck piece rather than the Saturday Evening Post printing itself — hence attributed rather than verified, and held below the promotion bar pending a human check against the printed interview.

Widely quoted and thoroughly consistent with Einstein's documented statements about intuition preceding reasoning (the Viereck interview, the Wertheimer conversations, the Hadamard survey on mathematical invention). But I cannot place a primary source for this exact sentence, and lines of this shape are exactly the kind that get retrofitted onto Einstein by inspirational compilers. I have a faint association with a mid-century popular biography, but it is too faint to print as a citation. Plausible but unverified.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Robert S. Marcus, 12 February 1950 (Albert Einstein Archives 60-424); widely reprinted, including in the New York Post, 28 November 1972
results.notes: The genuine article. Einstein wrote this in a condolence letter to Robert S. Marcus, political director of the World Jewish Congress, after the death of Marcus's son. The archival letter exists, which is why this passage survives scrutiny where its New Age paraphrases do not. Two small textual notes: the original reads 'a part of the whole' rather than 'a part of a whole' and 'widening our circles of compassion'; the ellipsis in the corpus text elides 'as something separated from the rest' into the following clause. Worth normalising against the archive text.

I am fairly confident this is genuine Einstein on death and the individual life. I associate it with his spoken credo of autumn 1932 ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis', recorded for the German League of Human Rights) and with the material collected in Dukas and Hoffmann's Albert Einstein: The Human Side. The variant wording I recall is closer to 'so much a part of everything living ... the concrete existence of any one person in this eternal flow', which suggests the corpus text is a different translation of the same German. Because I cannot settle which of those two sources carries it, I have left the print source null rather than guess between them.

This is a degraded paraphrase of the authentic 1950 letter to Robert S. Marcus, which the corpus already holds correctly as q_0260. The giveaways are 'self-imposed prison' and 'to find the reality of oneness' — neither phrase is in Einstein's letter; the original says the delusion 'is a kind of prison for us' and that our task is 'widening our circles of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.' The oneness formulation entered circulation through later spiritual literature. Recommendation for the human reviewer: this is a duplicate of q_0260 in corrupted form and should be dropped in favour of the archival wording, not promoted alongside it.

A loose popular restatement of the same Salaman-reported remark behind q_0257 ('I want to know how God created this world ... I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details', The Listener, 1955). The 'All I want to do is learn to think like God thinks' wording is not attested in Einstein's own words or in Salaman's account; it reads as a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Duplicative of q_0257, which is the better-supported form of the same line.

Long-standing and consistent attribution, and the vocabulary ('illimitable superior spirit', 'frail and feeble mind') matches Einstein's cosmic-religion register closely enough that I think it is genuine — compare the verified 1936 Phyllis Wright letter at q_0265, which says something very similar. I cannot place the primary document, however. It circulates in the standard Einstein compilations with varying and sometimes absent citations, and I do not want to pick one from memory. Probably genuine, source unplaced.

results.earliest_print_source: Letter to Phyllis Wright, 24 January 1936 (Albert Einstein Archives 42-601); reprinted in Albert Einstein: The Human Side, ed. Helen Dukas and Banesh Hoffmann
results.notes: Written to Phyllis Wright, a sixth-grade student at the Riverside Church in New York who had asked Einstein whether scientists pray. The archival letter is well documented and this passage is quoted from it accurately. Corpus text splits 'Every one' where the letter reads 'everyone', a trivial variant.

results.earliest_print_source: 'Religion and Science', The New York Times Magazine, 9 November 1930; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954)
results.notes: From Einstein's own signed essay 'Religion and Science', where he sets out the third stage of religious feeling — the cosmic religious sense of the scientist. A primary source in his own words. The corpus text matches the standard English printing.

results.earliest_print_source: The Metaphoric Mind: A Celebration of Creative Consciousness, Bob Samples, 1976
results.notes: A well-known misattribution and one I am confident about. Bob Samples wrote a loose gloss on Einstein — approximately 'Albert Einstein called the intuitive or metaphoric mind a sacred gift. He added that the rational mind was a faithful servant. It is paradoxical that in the context of modern life we have begun to worship the servant and defile the divine' — and that commentary was subsequently quoted back as if it were Einstein's own sentence. The 'sacred gift / faithful servant / honors the servant and has forgotten the gift' formulation is Samples' prose, not Einstein's, and no such passage exists in Einstein's writings. Recommend reattribution or removal.
results.suggested_reattribution: Bob Samples (paraphrasing Einstein)

results.notes: No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or reported conversations that I know of. It appears in late-twentieth-century quotation compilations attached to his name, which is the standard signature of an Einstein-magnet aphorism. I cannot identify a true origin either, so I am not offering a reattribution. Honest answer: unknown, and almost certainly not his.

results.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck interview with Einstein, 1929–1930 (published as 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929, and in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
results.notes: The child-in-the-library metaphor is genuinely Einstein's and is documented from his conversations with Viereck; the version I recall runs 'We are in the position of a little child entering a huge library whose walls are covered to the ceiling with books in many different tongues ... The child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books, a mysterious order which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects. That, it seems to me, is the attitude of the human mind, even the greatest and most cultured, toward God.' Caveats: the corpus text is a reported conversation, not something Einstein wrote, and its opening sentence ('The human mind is not capable of grasping the Universe') plus the truncated ending differ from the rendering I know. Attributed rather than verified because I cannot confirm which printing carries this exact wording.

results.earliest_print_source: Albert Einstein: The Human Side, ed. Helen Dukas and Banesh Hoffmann (1979)
results.notes: I recall this from the Dukas and Hoffmann collection of Einstein's personal correspondence, drawn from a letter or reply written in his last years (mid-1950s), and continuing past the ellipsis to say that this feeling has nothing to do with mysticism. Dukas was his secretary and the collection works from the archive, so the chain is good. Hedge: I am confident about the collection but not about the exact letter, recipient, or date, so I have named only the book and left the specifics out rather than invent them. Held below the promotion bar pending a page-level check.

Widely attributed to Einstein in quotation collections and compatible with his 'true religiosity' language, but I cannot place a primary source. The phrasing is noticeably plainer than his usual translated register, which makes me slightly wary that it is a paraphrase of a longer passage rather than a sentence he wrote. Not enough for me to call it misattributed, not nearly enough to promote. Uncertain.

results.earliest_print_source: "What I Believe", Albert Einstein, Forum and Century vol. 84 (1930); reprinted in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild (1934-35)
results.notes: Genuine Einstein passage from his 1930 credo essay 'What I Believe'. The canonical translation reads 'The most beautiful experience we can have is the mysterious. It is the fundamental emotion which stands at the cradle of true art and true science...' The wording here ('the finest emotion of which we are capable is the mystic emotion... the germ of all art and all true science') is a different, older English rendering that circulates widely, notably via Lincoln Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein (1948). Content, structure, and closing sentence ('in this sense, and in this sense alone, I rank myself among profoundly religious men') all match the authentic essay. Verified as Einstein; the exact English wording is translation-dependent.

Consistent with Einstein's 1930s social essays and commonly cited to him; I recall the line in the orbit of The World As I See It (1934) but cannot place the specific essay or page from memory, so I am not supplying a citation. Not one of the classic Einstein fakes (no self-help cadence, no science-vs-religion punchline), and the sentiment matches his repeated writing on the individual's obligation to community. Plausible but unconfirmed at the primary-source level.

results.earliest_print_source: LSD: My Problem Child (LSD - Mein Sorgenkind), Albert Hofmann, 1979 (English translation 1980)
results.notes: Authentic Hofmann, from LSD: My Problem Child - it appears in the framing material where he sets out why he wrote the book. The 'materialistic, dualistic belief that people and their environment are separate' / 'oneness with animate nature and all of creation' language is verbatim Hofmann and is one of the most-quoted passages in the book. NOTE: the author's name is misspelled in the corpus - it is Albert Hofmann (one 'f' at the end, two total), the Sandoz chemist who first synthesized LSD, not 'Albert Hoffman'.
results.suggested_reattribution: Albert Hofmann (spelling correction)

results.notes: This is a floating self-help aphorism with two competing attributions and no primary source under either. It is far more commonly attributed to William James ('The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes of mind'), and that James version is a known unverified attribution - it does not appear in James's published works and surfaces in mid-20th-century inspirational literature. The Schweitzer variant ('of any generation') looks like downstream drift from the James version. Neither attribution is supportable; I cannot identify the true originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

results.earliest_print_source: Civilization and Ethics (Kultur und Ethik), Albert Schweitzer, 1923 - The Philosophy of Civilization, Part II
results.notes: This is Schweitzer's core statement of Ehrfurcht vor dem Leben (reverence for life) and is a genuine passage from his ethics volume, where he defines the ethical man as one for whom all life is sacred and who helps all life in need. Schweitzer restates it in Out of My Life and Thought (1931). Confident in the author and the work; slight residual uncertainty only on chapter/page and translation wording.

This is a loose paraphrase of a line widely attributed to Schweitzer in the form 'I don't know what your destiny will be, but one thing I know: the only ones among you who will be really happy are those who will have sought and found how to serve.' Even that canonical form has no confirmed primary source - it is usually reported secondhand as advice to students, without a traceable speech or text. The wording given here ('what path in life you will take... you will never be happy') is a further-degraded retelling. The sentiment is authentically Schweitzerian, but neither the wording nor the source can be verified.

Genuinely Schweitzer's, to the best of my knowledge; the standard translation runs 'Sometimes our light goes out but is blown into flame again by an encounter with another human being. Each of us owes deepest thanks to those who have rekindled this inner light.' I recall it being sourced to Memoirs of Childhood and Youth (1924), but I am not confident enough in that placement to record it as a citation. The version in the corpus is a rephrasing ('our inner fire goes out', 'burst into flame'). Attribution good, exact source and wording unconfirmed.

A signature Szent-Gyorgyi line, consistently attributed to him across scientific and popular literature and entirely in his idiom. It is usually sourced to his contribution to I. J. Good's anthology The Scientist Speculates (1962), but I cannot confirm that placement precisely enough to record it as a citation. NOTE: the author's name is garbled in the corpus - the correct form is Albert Szent-Gyorgyi (Hungarian Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine, 1937; full name Albert von Szent-Gyorgyi Nagyrapolt), not 'Albert von Szent-Gyorgy'.
results.suggested_reattribution: Albert Szent-Gyorgyi (spelling correction)

results.notes: I cannot place this in Huxley's work, and the aphoristic snap of it is unlike his prose, which is discursive even when epigrammatic. It sits in a family of interchangeable aging aphorisms whose attributions rotate freely - compare 'Nobody grows old merely by living a number of years; we grow old by deserting our ideals' (Samuel Ullman) and 'We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing' (attributed variously to Oliver Wendell Holmes and George Bernard Shaw, unverified in both). No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know who said it.

Authentic Huxley, from the last years of his life (c. 1961-62) - the self-deprecating cadence and the phrase 'the human problem' are characteristic, and the remark is well documented in the Huxley literature as a summing-up he offered near the end. It is usually reported from a late lecture or interview rather than from something he wrote, and I cannot fix the specific occasion or the secondary source that first printed it, so I am leaving the citation null. Attribution strong, provenance of the report unconfirmed.

results.earliest_print_source: Texts and Pretexts: An Anthology with Commentaries, Aldous Huxley, 1932
results.notes: Genuine Huxley, from the opening pages of Texts and Pretexts. Original wording: 'Experience is not what happens to a man; it is what a man does with what happens to him.' The corpus version is a modernized second-person rendering of the same sentence. Frequently misattributed elsewhere to Carl Jung and to Anthony Robbins-style paraphrasers, but Huxley is the source.

results.earliest_print_source: "A Case of Voluntary Ignorance", Aldous Huxley, in Collected Essays (1959); essay first published 1956
results.notes: Authentic Huxley, from the essay 'A Case of Voluntary Ignorance', collected in Collected Essays (1959) after appearing in his mid-1950s essay work. The self-swallowing structure of the sentence is quoted accurately in the corpus. Confident in author and essay; mild uncertainty on first-publication venue and date.

This is Huxley's central thesis about means and ends and reads as authentically his - the argument that means determine ends is the spine of his 1937 book Ends and Means, written under Gerald Heard's and the pacifist movement's influence. The standard attribution points to Ends and Means (1937), but I cannot confirm this exact sentence pair appears there rather than in a related essay or in his Gandhi commentary, so I am not recording a citation. Attribution to Huxley is sound; the specific work is unconfirmed.

Alex Grey is a living visionary artist and the passage is squarely in his register - the cosmic-evolutionary framing of creativity and the phrase 'the redemptive mission of art' echo his book The Mission of Art (1998) and his lecture material. But I cannot place this specific wording in a published text or talk, and contemporary artist statements circulate heavily paraphrased on social media. Plausibly authentic, unconfirmed.

Standardly attributed to Alexandre Dumas fils in 20th-century quotation dictionaries ('Toutes les generalisations sont dangereuses, y compris celle-ci'), but I know of no primary source in his plays or novels, and quotation dictionaries of that era propagated attributions without sourcing. A close cousin, 'No generalization is wholly true, not even this one', is attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes - the two may share an origin or may be independent formulations of an old joke. NOTE: if this attribution is kept, the corpus name should be 'Alexandre Dumas' (fils), not the anglicized 'Alexander Dumas'.

I cannot place this in either Dumas pere or Dumas fils. It circulates on aggregator sites credited to a bare 'Alexandre Dumas', which is a common pattern for orphaned motivational lines - the enlist-against-yourself conceit reads more like 19th-century moralist or later self-help prose than like Dumas's narrative voice, though I would not call it a misattribution without evidence of a different author. No traceable source. NOTE: the corpus name is anglicized ('Alexander'); the French author is Alexandre Dumas, and which Dumas is intended is itself unclear.

This reaches modern readers through Napoleon Hill, who quotes it as Alexander Graham Bell in Think and Grow Rich (1937) - I am fairly but not fully confident of that placement, so I have not recorded it as a citation. The material point is that Hill is an unreliable transmitter: his claimed interviews with and quotations from Carnegie, Edison, Bell and others have been repeatedly challenged, and several are undocumented outside his own books. I know of no Bell letter, lecture, or notebook containing this sentence. Treat the attribution as weak pending a primary source.

Alexander Isley is a real and identifiable graphic designer (founding art director of Spy magazine, later Alexander Isley Inc.), and the line has the flavor of design-school advice given in an AIGA talk or a published list of maxims for young designers - the kind of source that rarely makes it into quotation records. I cannot confirm the wording or the occasion. Attribution plausible and specific enough not to look invented, but unverified.

Very likely genuine Pope, from the aphorism collection Thoughts on Various Subjects (first published 1727 in the Pope-Swift Miscellanies), where the sentence runs closer to 'Some people will never learn anything, for this reason, because they understand everything too soon.' Two caveats keep this below verified: the Miscellanies were a joint Pope-Swift production and individual maxims are sometimes disputed between them, and the corpus text is a compressed modernization with an ellipsis rather than the original wording.

results.earliest_print_source: An Essay on Criticism, Alexander Pope, 1711 (Part II, line 525)
results.notes: One of the best-documented lines in English poetry. Pope's couplet reads 'Good-nature and good-sense must ever join; / To err is human, to forgive, divine.' Primary source is unambiguous.

results.earliest_print_source: The Gulag Archipelago 1918-1956, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, 1973 (Volume 1, Part I, Chapter 4, "The Bluecaps")
results.notes: Authentic and correctly quoted, from the celebrated passage in 'The Bluecaps'. The full passage continues past what is quoted here ('During the life of any heart this line keeps changing place...'). Text matches the Whitney/Willetts English translation closely. NOTE: the corpus uses the anglicized 'Alexander'; the standard transliteration is Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.

results.earliest_print_source: Dialogues of Alfred North Whitehead, as recorded by Lucien Price, 1954
results.notes: Genuine Whitehead, recorded by Lucien Price. The full remark is 'There are no whole truths; all truths are half-truths. It is trying to treat them as whole truths that plays the devil.' The corpus quotes only the middle clause, which is the form that circulates. Source is a recorded conversation rather than Whitehead's own pen, but Price's Dialogues is an accepted and dated primary record.

results.earliest_print_source: Adventures of Ideas, Alfred North Whitehead, 1933
results.notes: Consistent with Whitehead's treatment of Adventure as a civilizing force in the final part of Adventures of Ideas, where he argues that art and civilization decay without the sense of adventure. I am confident in the author and reasonably confident in the book; the exact wording circulates in two forms ('when there is' / 'where there is'), which suggests some paraphrase drift, so I am holding this just under the verified bar rather than claiming chapter and page.

Almost certainly not Whitehead. The flippant one-liner register is entirely foreign to his prose, and the theological claim contradicts his actual position: Whitehead's process theology in Process and Reality (1929) and Religion in the Making (1926) develops a dipolar God distinct from, though internally related to, the world - he had no interest in the human-as-deity conceit, and he was not an atheist earlier in life in the sense the joke requires. This reads as a modern quip or bumper-sticker line that acquired a philosopher's name for weight. I cannot identify the actual originator, so no reattribution is offered. Recommend removal rather than reassignment.

results.earliest_print_source: Preface to The Dreaded Comparison: Human and Animal Slavery by Marjorie Spiegel, Alice Walker, 1988
results.notes: Authentic Alice Walker, from the preface she wrote for Marjorie Spiegel's The Dreaded Comparison. The parallel she draws between animal exploitation and the ideologies of racial slavery and patriarchy is the explicit argument of that preface, and this is its most-quoted sentence. Correctly attributed and accurately quoted.

Consistently attributed to Alice Walker in quote collections and I have a weak recollection of it appearing in her fiction (possibly The Temple of My Familiar, 1989), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific work with confidence. No competing claimant, so the attribution is plausible; the sourcing is not established.

Widely and consistently attributed to Alice Walker, and the aphoristic-theological turn is characteristic of her essays. I cannot identify the book, essay, or interview it comes from, so I will not name one. Plausible but unsourced.

One of the most-circulated Alice Walker lines, attributed to her with unusual consistency and no rival claimant, which is mild evidence in its favor. But it circulates without a source citation everywhere I have seen it; I cannot place it in a specific book, essay, or speech. Attribution likely correct, provenance unestablished.

Attributed to Alina Wheeler (author of Designing Brand Identity) in most design-quote contexts, but the same line is also circulated as Le Corbusier's, and I cannot confirm either. If it is Wheeler's it would most plausibly come from Designing Brand Identity, but I cannot confirm that it originates with her rather than being quoted by her. Competing attribution keeps confidence low.

I have no knowledge of an author named Allyson Jones associated with this or any quotation, and no recollection of the line itself. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know where this came from or whether the attributed person exists as a public author.

results.earliest_print_source: Future Shock, Alvin Toffler, 1970 (quoting psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy)
results.notes: Toffler did not originate this. In Future Shock (1970) he quotes psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy: 'The illiterate of the future will not be the person who cannot read. The widely circulated '21st century / learn, unlearn, and relearn' wording is a later popular reshaping of that sentence, not a verbatim Toffler line. Toffler is the transmitter, Gerjuoy the source of the thought; the exact modern wording is of uncertain authorship.

results.notes: Very widely attributed to Earhart and consistent with her documented voice on risk and resolve; I believe it derives from her own writing or correspondence, but I cannot place it in a specific book (The Fun of It, Last Flight) or letter, so I will not cite one. Plausible and uncontested, but unsourced in what I know.

I suspect an older, uncredited source that has been re-labelled with a famous name, but I cannot identify that source, so I am not proposing a reattribution. Treat the Earhart attribution as doubtful.

Consistently attributed to Earhart and strongly consistent with her documented statements about accepting the hazards of her flights (compare the pre-1937 'popping-off' letter to G.P. Putnam). This is a modern internet aphorism with a snappy cadence unlike Earhart's prose, and I know of no source for it in her writings, letters, or contemporary press. Earhart is a magnet for aspirational lines of this kind. Related but distinct older sayings exist (e.g. John Andrew Holmes on never telling a young person a thing cannot be done). Attribution should be treated as very likely apocryphal; I stop short of the 'apocryphal' label only because I cannot demonstrate invention.

results.earliest_print_source: Seduction of the Minotaur, Anaïs Nin, 1961
results.notes: Nin did write a version of this in Seduction of the Minotaur (1961), but she presented it as a saying she was recalling, framed as Talmudic ('we do not see things as they are, we see them as we are'). The maxim is older than Nin and is not actually in the Talmud; variants circulated in English well before 1961. So Nin is a real conduit but not the originator, and the corpus should not present her as the author without that caveat. I cannot name the earliest English printing with confidence.

Consistently cited as Nin's and stylistically hers; standard citations place it in The Diary of Anaïs Nin, though I cannot confirm which volume, so I have not named one. No competing attribution known.

Universally attributed to Nin and usually circulated as part of a short piece titled 'Risk', but its location in her published corpus is contested — I recall ongoing disagreement about whether it appears in the diaries as printed. Note also that the wording here ('There came a time when...') differs from the standard circulating form ('And the day came when the risk to remain tight in a bud...'), which is a marker of a quote that has drifted. Attribution plausible, source not established.

results.earliest_print_source: The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 3 (1939–1944), Anaïs Nin
results.notes: The best-sourced of the Nin lines in this batch: standard references place it in the third volume of the published Diary, in an early-1940s entry, and the attribution is stable across sources. I am citing the volume from recollection of consistent standard citations rather than a checked page, so I hold it just under the primary-source band.

Consistently attributed to Nin and consistent with her recurring reflections on why she kept the diary. Commonly cited to the published Diary (a later volume), but I cannot confirm the volume or the exact wording of the original sentence, and the popular form may be a tightening of a longer passage. No competing claimant.

results.earliest_print_source: Nadja, André Breton, 1928
results.notes: The closing line of Nadja (1928): 'La beauté sera CONVULSIVE ou ne sera pas.' Primary source is secure. The English here is a compressed rendering — the literal sense is 'Beauty will be CONVULSIVE or it will not be [at all]'; the corpus may want the standard translation wording.

results.earliest_print_source: Les Faux-Monnayeurs (The Counterfeiters), André Gide, 1925
results.notes: Genuine Gide, from The Counterfeiters (1925): 'On ne découvre pas de terre nouvelle sans consentir à perdre de vue, d'abord et pour longtemps, tout rivage.' The English here is a faithful translation. This is the authentic original of which q_0314 is the popular corruption.

This popular English wording does not correspond to any sentence Gide wrote. It is a loose, anonymous paraphrase of the Counterfeiters line captured verbatim in q_0313 ('new lands' / 'lose sight of the shore' becoming 'new oceans' / 'courage'). Gide is the source of the thought, not of these words, and the paraphraser is unknown. The corpus already holds the authentic version at q_0313 and should prefer it; this entry is a duplicate in corrupted form.
results.suggested_reattribution: Paraphrase of André Gide, Les Faux-Monnayeurs (1925); paraphraser unknown

results.earliest_print_source: Les Nourritures terrestres (The Fruits of the Earth), André Gide, 1897
results.notes: From the closing envoi of The Fruits of the Earth, addressed to Nathanaël. Standard translations end 'the most irreplaceable of beings' rather than 'of things', and the passage as given has been trimmed of its direct address to Nathanaël — worth normalizing against a published translation.
